title: Tool output fidelity tradeoffs and SDK guidelines (draft)
content:
Goal:
Provide a pragmatic set of SDK ergonomics and server-side behavior for delivering progressive (low-latency) streaming responses while preserving structured tool-calls and a clear fidelity contract for clients and integrators. This doc focuses on tradeoffs and concrete SDK surface proposals rather than final wire-format decisions.

Context / rationale:
- Customers build latency-sensitive experiences (summaries, chat, copilots) that need early partial output to keep UI snappy.
- Many integrations require the model to call external tools (search, calendar, calculators) and emit structured payloads. Tool-calls must be reliable and detectable even when partial streaming is in flight.
- There is a tension: aggressive early streaming increases perceived responsiveness but may expose partial/low-fidelity tokens that break deterministic tool-call detection or produce malformed structured output.
- SDK ergonomics should make it natural for app developers to opt into lower-latency progressive modes without risking silent data loss or compatibility surprises.

Key product constraints:
- Backwards compatibility with existing hosted API call shapes (text + streaming boundary semantics).
- Support server-side aborts/fallbacks and explicit canary rollouts of streaming fidelity features.
- Metricability: we must surface token-level fidelity metrics (confidence markers, structured parse rates) to customers via Console.

Design principles:
1) Explicit fidelity lanes: server annotates streaming frames with a small set of fidelity markers (draft|confirmed|tool-call-final) so clients can decide how to render partial content.
2) Structured-first heartbeat: keep a thin structured event channel (SEV) in the stream dedicated to tool-calls, schema chunks, and end-of-entity markers. Text tokens remain in a separate channel.
3) Graceful degradation: when network/server constraints force lower-fidelity outputs, emit clear signals and provide deterministic fallbacks (e.g., final API reconciliation endpoint).
4) Minimal SDK surprise: default SDK should favor correctness (delay structured output rendering until tool-call-final) while exposing opt-ins for progressive UX.

Streaming frames and semantics (proposal):
- frame.type = text | struct | meta
- frame.fidelity = draft | confirmed | final
- text frames: token runs intended for human rendering; may include interim punctuation.
- struct frames: JSON-LD-like small objects carrying tool-call intents, call args, and schema fragments. Must be parseable even mid-stream.
- meta frames: progress markers, truncation warnings, sequence ids for multi-part responses.

Fidelity lanes explained:
- draft: earliest tokens; high chance of being revised. Clients should show as "loading" or ephemeral.
- confirmed: model has higher internal certainty (longer context); safe for progressive display in many apps.
- final: server considers emitted content stable for downstream processing and tool invocation.
- tool-call-final (subclass of final): indicates that a tool-call payload has been committed and can be executed by a client or backend without reconciliation.

SDK ergonomics (JS + Python surfaces):
Default behavior (safe):
- on('text') -> receives only confirmed/final text frames. Draft frames are internally buffered and not emitted to callback unless opt-in enabled.
- on('struct') -> receives only tool-call-final frames. Partial struct frames are visible via a separate on('struct-draft') callback for debugging only.
- fetchOutput() -> returns the final reconciled output (blocking or async) and a structured list of tool-calls that were committed.

Progressive behavior (opt-in):
- enableProgressive = true -> client gets on('text-draft') and on('struct-draft') callbacks. SDK also surfaces a small API to mark UI rendering intent: renderMode: inline | banner | ephemeral.
- progressiveToolRouting: when enabled, SDK emits tool-call-final as soon as available and may speculatively trigger configured tool adapters. There must be a confirmToolExecution(toolId, executionId) call to reconcile in case the server later retracts.

Backpressure and client-side flow control:
- SDK exposes setClientBudget(milliseconds) so UIs can throttle draft emissions for slow clients.
- Server attempts to honor client budget but may downgrade fidelity (emit more drafts) under high load; meta frames will explain the downgrade reason.

Structured output schema strategy:
- Minimal schema footprint: server sends schema hints (type, required fields) ahead of the structured payload when possible.
- Chunked schema transfer: for large tool-call args, struct frames can carry 'schema-part-N' with sequence ids; SDK will assemble and validate.
- Lenient parser: default SDK parser should be tolerant of trailing commas and unterminated chunks in draft mode and only strict-validate on tool-call-final.

Telemetry and observability hooks (Console needs):
- token_fidelity_histogram per model+route
- struct_commit_rate: fraction of struct frames that reach final commit
- avg_time_to_tool-call-final (ms)
- draft_display_rate: fraction of client sessions that opted into progressive drafts
- reconciliation_events: counts and examples of tool-call retractions

Safety and security notes:
- Tool-call-final is the only signal that should be trusted to auto-execute side effects; until final, treat payloads as speculative.
- SDKs must surface a clear warning in telemetry when speculative execution is enabled.
- For hosted Enterprise customers with stricter risk tolerance, default to conservative behavior (no speculative tool execution, only final commits).

Compatibility and migration path:
1) Phase 1 (beta): server emits new frame types but SDKs only surface confirmed/final by default. Beta customers can opt into progressive lanes via feature flag.
2) Phase 2 (wider rollout): console exposes per-customer defaults and policy toggles for speculative execution and draft rendering.
3) Phase 3 (opt-out sunset): validated stable clients may enable progressive-by-default with explicit guardrails in account settings.

Open questions / tradeoffs to resolve:
- How large should draft text buffer be before the SDK emits anything? (size vs latency)
- Do we need separate event channel for schema vs tool-call payloads, or can we multiplex?
- How to represent streaming retractions that change previously emitted tool-call args without confusing downstream tool adapters?
- UX surface for reconciliation: how do we present that a tool-call was "retracted" after the app already acted?
- Billing implications: do we charge three-way (draft tokens vs final tokens) or keep current single token model?

Action items / next steps:
- [Owner: Marisol] Draft wire-level examples for Go/JS/Python SDKs (due 2025-12-12).
- [Owner: Ethan] Prototype a streaming trace in the Console that highlights fidelity lanes end-to-end (due 2025-12-05).
- [Owner: Priya] Run customer interviews with three latency-sensitive partners to validate progressive rendering preferences (due 2025-12-08).
- [Owner: Jonas] Spike on a tolerant struct-parser implementation and sample metrics (due 2025-12-11).

Appendix: example pseudo-stream (abbreviated)
- meta: {seq:1, mode:progressive}
- text(draft): "Here is a quick overview of the..."
- struct(draft): {intent:"search", q_part: "what is the latest"}
- text(confirmed): "latest release notes show"
- struct(final, tool-call-final): {intent:"search", q: "what is the latest release notes for product X", id: "call-37"}
- meta: {seq:END, reconciled:true}

Notes to reviewers:
- Please call out places where server-side complexity might be better handled in the SDK (or vice-versa).
- Think about mobile clients with intermittent connectivity — we need to avoid making draft rendering the default there.
- Suggest realistic guardrails for speculative execution that are easy for customers to understand in Console settings.

Status: early draft; looking for engineering pushback on bandwidth/backpressure assumptions and SRE input on reliability under load.
